claims.text: Selective dealloying of a homogeneous HEA precursor can reliably produce three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
Dealloying preferentially dissolves the less noble components of an HEA precursor.
Preferential dissolution concentrates the noble metals into an interconnected porous network.
The resulting porous network provides enhanced catalytic surface area.
The proposed precursor is a uniformly mixed atomic-scale solid solution containing noble and less noble elements.
Chemical or electrochemical dealloying can selectively remove less noble elements without significantly attacking the noble-metal framework.
Selective dissolution triggers reorganization of the remaining noble-metal atoms into a three-dimensional interconnected network.
Differences in chemical or electrochemical potential cause less noble metals to leach from the HEA under controlled dealloying conditions.
Surface diffusion and reassembly of the remaining noble-metal atoms produce a porous three-dimensional nanoframework.
The dealloyed three-dimensional nanoframework maintains atomic-scale mixing.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframework has greater surface area than bulk or nonporous HEA structures.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframework preserves atomic-level mixing.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframework has improved catalytic properties relative to bulk or nonporous HEA structures.
Conventional HEA synthesis methods such as melt casting and sputtering typically produce bulk or thin-film materials lacking high surface porosity.
Effective selective dealloying requires sufficient differences in corrosion or dissolution potential among precursor constituents.
Small differences in constituent dissolution potentials can make selective removal ineffective.
